widget.prompt: Answer aloud first, in under two minutes, then write the story as you told it. The question: "Tell me about a project you owned." Use a phone timer; nothing is recorded. Use STAR from l11 and end with one line of reflection. Then mark it against the rubric.
widget.model:
**Nadia: a project you owned.** Nadia is an invented candidate: a maths student, class of 2029, aiming at trading. Setting: a project. About 178 words, about 1 minute 22 seconds aloud at 130 words a minute.

Last spring I wanted to know if a simple momentum rule still works after trading costs. Nobody set it: it was my own project, on 20 years of monthly prices for UK shares. My task was to give an honest answer, not a flattering one. First I wrote the backtest in Python and pandas, buying the past year's winners and selling the losers each month. The first run showed a Sharpe ratio of 1.3, which looked too good. So I checked every date and found a look-ahead bug. I was using each month's closing price to choose that same month's trades. I fixed it by lagging the signal by one month, and the Sharpe fell to 0.9. Then I added a cost of 10 basis points a trade, and it fell again, to 0.4. I wrote a one-page note with the code, so anyone could rerun it. The result was a modest, honest answer: momentum survives costs here, but only just. I learned to distrust a result that looks too good until I have tried to break it.

Why it scores 10:
- the situation takes two sentences
- the task is hers
- each action starts with "I"
- the result has numbers
- the last line says what she learned
- it is under 260 words
- it answers the question asked

**Nadia: a failure.** Nadia is an invented candidate: a maths student, class of 2029, aiming at trading. Setting: study. About 150 words, about 1 minute 9 seconds aloud at 130 words a minute.

In January of my first year I sat a probability exam worth a quarter of the module. I had aimed for 70%, the mark for a First, and I scored 52%. The failure was mine: I had read my notes many times but done almost no problems against the clock. My task was to fix my method before the June exam, which counted for the rest. First I asked the lecturer where I had lost marks; most were on conditional probability. Then I changed how I revised: three timed past papers a week, marked the same day. I kept a list of every mistake and redid each one a week later. By May my timed scores had risen from about 50% to about 70%. In June I scored 71%, and the module ended at 66%. I learned that reading is not practice, so now I time myself on every topic.

items.question: Write this as you will tell it.

widget.prompt: Answer aloud first, in under two minutes, then write the story as you told it. The question: "Tell me about a time you made a decision without all the facts." Use a phone timer; nothing is recorded. Use STAR from l11 and end with one line of reflection. Then mark it against the rubric.
widget.model:
**Nadia: a decision with incomplete information.** Nadia is an invented candidate: a maths student, class of 2029, aiming at trading. Setting: a contest. About 168 words, about 1 minute 18 seconds aloud at 130 words a minute.

Last November my team of three entered a university trading game. Over one afternoon we traded a made-up company's shares while news arrived in five releases. I was the one who set our position size. After the third release the shares had risen from £70 to £100. We had to decide with two releases still to come. My teammates wanted the maximum, 100 shares, because the news so far was good. I did not know what the last two releases held. So I worked out our loss if the price fell back to £70: £3,000 of our £10,000 game money. I argued for half size, 50 shares, and said I would add more if the fourth release agreed. It did not: the fourth release was bad and the price dropped 15%, to £85. Because we held half, we lost £750 instead of £1,500, and we finished 3rd of 24 teams. I learned to size a decision by what I do not know, not only by what I do.

**Nadia: working in a team.** Nadia is an invented candidate: a maths student, class of 2029, aiming at trading. Setting: a sports team. About 155 words, about 1 minute 12 seconds aloud at 130 words a minute.

This year I captain my university's second netball team, ten players in all. We had lost five of our first six matches, and most goals against us came late. As captain, my task was to find out why and change it before the second half of the season. I went through the score sheets and found we conceded 60% of our goals in the final quarter. I suspected fitness, so I asked each player privately how training felt. Three said the sessions were too long and too late. I proposed moving training from 9 pm to 6 pm and adding ten minutes of sprints. I put it to a vote. Eight of the ten voted for it. I also set up a rota so two substitutes came on in every quarter. We won six of our last eight matches. I learned that asking people one by one tells me more than asking the whole group.

widget.prompt: Answer aloud first, in under two minutes, then write the story as you told it. The question: "Tell me about a time you disagreed with someone." Use a phone timer; nothing is recorded. Use STAR from l11 and end with one line of reflection. Then mark it against the rubric.
widget.model:
**Nadia: a disagreement.** Nadia is an invented candidate: a maths student, class of 2029, aiming at trading. Setting: a part-time job. About 170 words, about 1 minute 18 seconds aloud at 130 words a minute.

I work part-time as a shift supervisor in a café near campus. Last winter the manager wanted to cut the evening shift from two staff to one, to save wages. I disagreed: I thought evenings were busier than she believed. Her side was fair: wages are the café's biggest cost, and the evening till totals looked low. My task was to settle it with facts, not opinions. For two weeks I logged sales by the hour from the till. The data showed 6 pm to 8 pm was our second-busiest window, but 8 pm to close was quiet. So I proposed a split: two staff until 8 pm, then one. I also used the hourly data to bake less for the evening. So weekly food waste fell from £120 to £70. The manager kept the split rota, and we saved most of the wages she wanted to save. I learned to bring data to a disagreement. I learned to look for the part of the other view that is right.

widget.prompt: Answer aloud first, in under two minutes, then write the story as you told it. The question: "Tell me about a time you had to learn something fast." Use a phone timer; nothing is recorded. Use STAR from l11 and end with one line of reflection. Then mark it against the rubric.
widget.model:
**Nadia: pressure or learning something fast.** Nadia is an invented candidate: a maths student, class of 2029, aiming at trading. Setting: a society. About 155 words, about 1 minute 12 seconds aloud at 130 words a minute.

In my first year, our poker society's treasurer left two weeks before our biggest tournament of the term. I volunteered to take over, though I had never kept accounts. My task was to collect 60 entry fees, pay for the room and prizes, and leave the books right. On the first night I read the last two years of the society's spreadsheets and listed every kind of payment. I asked the students' union finance officer to check my plan, which took her twenty minutes. Then I built one sheet that matched every payment to a line on the bank statement. On the night, I took fees by card only, so each one left a record. The tournament came in £35 under its £150 budget. When the union audited the society in March, our books had no errors. I learned that when I must learn fast, I find the person who already knows and ask early.

- each action starts with "I"
- the result has numbers
- the last line says what she learned

items.question: "On average, how many rolls of a fair die until a 5 or a 6?" Put the moves of reasoning aloud in order. Leave out the one that does not belong.

lines.text: Restate: we roll until a 5 or a 6 and count the rolls.
Assume: the die is fair and the rolls are independent.
Anchor: a third of rolls succeed, so roughly 3.
Summarise: 3 rolls, at least 1, and it matches the anchor.
Write the answer down silently, then explain it at the end.
lines.why: You kept the silent working. The interviewer cannot follow or steer it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each move uses the one before it.

byKey.silent: You kept the silent working. A method the interviewer cannot hear cannot be marked.
byKey.left-out: You left out a move that belongs. Only the silent working goes.

explain.text: One roll always happens, and with chance $\tfrac23$ we start again, so $E = 1 + \tfrac23 E$ and $E = 3$. The anchor, a third of rolls succeed, predicted it. Say every move aloud (l12).

items.question: A trading firm offers you an internship on 1 March, with a deadline of 15 March. The bank you prefer decides on 20 March. Select all that apply: which are good moves?

options.text: Thank the firm and confirm the deadline in writing
Tell the bank on 1 or 2 March and ask whether it can speed up
If it cannot, ask the firm once to reply by 21 March, giving the reason
Accept the firm now and renege if the bank says yes
options.why: You planned to renege. Accepting is a promise.

options.text: Let 15 March pass and wait to be chased
options.why: You let the deadline lapse. The offer can simply be withdrawn.

options.text: Tell the firm the bank pays more, to push it
options.why: You bargained with a claim. It reads as a threat, and bank pay is usually lower (l14).

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the moves that keep both firms' trust.

explain.text: Thanking and confirming fixes the clock; telling the bank at once gives it about two weeks to move. One polite request, with a reason and a date, is easy to grant. Reneging and silence both break the offer's rules (l14).

widget.prompt: Optional. Write your plan for a final-round day: the day before, the day itself and the evening after. Include the time and place or link, what you bring and your reset between rounds. Add two questions for each round and what you write down afterwards. Use l13's checklist as a start.

**Nadia's final-round plan** (an invented candidate; the firm is invented too). Her day: four 45-minute rounds in the office, 9:30 to 14:15, with lunch.

**The day before**

| When | What | Done |
|---|---|---|
| 10:00 | Confirm the time, address and the recruiter's number by email | ✓ |
| 11:00 | Plan the journey: train at 7:52, arrive 8:55; a later train at 8:22 as backup | ✓ |
| 14:00 | Print two CVs; write the six story cue words on one card | ✓ |
| 16:00 | Write two questions for each round | ✓ |
| 21:00 | Stop work; lay out clothes; sleep by 22:30 | ✓ |

**Questions to ask.**
- Probability round: "What does a good answer sound like here?" and "Which question do candidates find hardest?"
- Market making: "How do new traders learn to size?" and "How is an intern's trading judged?"
- Coding: "What do interns own by the last week?" and "How is code reviewed on the team?"
- Behavioural: "What surprised you when you joined?" and "What do the best interns do differently?"

**On the day.** Breakfast at 7:15. Between rounds: water, one breath, one line on paper, then put it away. If a round goes badly, I do not mention it in the next one. At lunch I eat, and I do not revise.

**If it is remote.** Camera at eye level with a lamp in front, door shut and phone in a drawer. Paper and pen on the desk, and the recruiter's number on a sticky note.

**Afterwards.** That evening I write down every question from each round and one line on how it went. I send a short thank-you to the recruiter the next morning.
